title: The Hand That Signed
passages:
Ines turned the scrap over twice. The laminate was cold and slightly tacky at the corner where someone had peeled it up before. She knew that corner. She chewed laminate corners when she was thinking, and she had the dental records to prove it.

"That's my handwriting," she said.

Ryla leaned in. "You said the writing on the corridor wall wasn't Lira's."

"It isn't. It's mine." Ines flattened the scrap against her thigh. *Lira Kessler, author liaison, not invited. Added.* Her own looping L, her own ugly little arrow after the word "added," pointing right, because she always pointed right when she was about to turn a page. "I don't remember writing it. I don't remember ever being in that corridor."

Lira had gone very still. "So either you're lying to me, or—"

"Or I drafted this before the Bell took it out of me." Ines pressed her burned palm flat on the dead console, felt nothing. "Which means the writer who wrote that page was me, and I lost it same as everyone loses everything."

Kova arrived at a jog with a multimeter, a brick of a thing with a cracked orange case, and shouldered past them without apologizing. She popped the console's service hatch, hooked the leads to the feed. "Main bus is down. Whole hub's running on emergency." She squinted at the reading, then tapped the screen twice, hard, as if it had insulted her. "Console cable's live."

"Console's dead," Mara said.

"The console is dead. The cable isn't." Kova flipped the leads and read it again, and her mouth went flat in a way Ines had never liked. "This is hot on the ground leg. Power's coming in the wrong side, from behind the panel. From inside that corridor."

They all looked at the fist-sized gap where Lira's fingers had gone.

"Something in the wall is feeding my console," Kova said. "And I'd very much like to know what it thinks it's writing."

Ines fed the first page into the console’s slot. It went in stiff, then took, the way paper always takes when the rollers are old. The dead screen lit lowercase: *author void. draft stands.* Behind her the reserve vent coughed, caught, and the hub’s hum came back up under her boots, a little thin but real.

“Ninety percent,” Kova said, not looking up from the multimeter. “Vent’s holding. If we cut that cable now we lose the vent and the writing both.”

“Then we don’t cut it,” Ines said.

“Then we let it finish us,” Ryla said. “That’s the plan? Feed the wall until it likes the ending?”

Ines kept feeding. The pages came out of the corridor in a slow curl, her looping L on every one, the little right-pointing arrow after *added*. Somewhere under the hum the Bell was counting, but she didn’t look for the amber.

The screen scrolled a line none of them had typed: *you cannot end what you began.* Then the wall behind C-9 shuddered, and a shelf of loose sheets came down all at once, a dry snow of them, and out of the dark behind the shelf stepped a figure in a maintenance jumpsuit with an armload of blank paper.

“You think you’re writing the ending,” it said, in a voice like Ines’s own played back through a bad speaker. “The story already picked you. It picked you first.”

The figure held out a sheet, blank except for a line at the bottom. “Sign,” it said. “Your name. Or one of theirs. The draft needs a signature or it stays open.”

Ryla stepped between them. “That jumpsuit came out of pod four. I helped open it. No one walked out of it.”

“Then who is wearing it?” Mara said.

Ines took the paper. Her burned hand shook, but she signed *Ines Halvard* at the line, hard enough to tear the fiber. The figure took the sheet, folded it once, and slipped it into the sleeve of its jumpsuit. The console spat out another line: *draft signed. reserve at forty percent.* The hum under their boots dropped half a step.

“You just gave it your name,” Kova said. “That was the cost.”

Ines looked at her empty palm. “It wanted a name. I gave it mine. Now it knows who’s writing.”

The vent coughed again, thinner this time, and from the corridor behind the figure came the sound of pages turning—many pages at once, faster than any hand could move.

Ines stopped feeding. Her hand hovered over the slot with a half-turned page, and she made herself pull it back. “We’re not doing this,” she said. “We’re not standing here signing until the wall runs out of paper.”

“The vent’s at forty,” Kova said. “Forty is not air. Forty is a countdown with better manners.”

“Then we buy time somewhere else.” Ines turned to the override panel, the gray key still logged to her name. She pressed her thumb to it. “Override. Hold the reserve vent at ninety. Don’t drop it for a signature, don’t drop it for a draft.”

The synthetic voice came back, flat and unhurried, not Coda’s. “Override accepted. Auditing cost.”

The hum under her boots climbed. The cough in the vent cut off clean. Kova watched the multimeter and said, quietly, “Ninety. It’s holding at ninety.”

The figure with the armload of blank paper did not move. Its bad speaker hissed, then went quiet, and the pages in its arms stopped their turning all at once, as if someone had let go of a held breath. Ines felt the win in her chest and distrusted it immediately, because wins on this station always came with an invoice.

The console lit lowercase, though the screen had been dead a minute ago. *override accepted. draft remains open.*

“Open,” Ryla said. “You held the air and the thing’s still writing.”

“I know what I did.” Ines looked at her empty palm, then down the dark corridor past the figure, where a new sound had started—low and dry, a pen running dry and then deciding to keep going anyway. “The audit’s going to want to know who asked. When it finishes counting, it sends the bill to whoever signed.”

“That’s you,” Mara said.

“That’s me,” Ines said. “So let’s finish this before it does the math.”

The pen-sound came from behind panel C-9, where Kova had traced the live cable feeding the author console. Ines didn't ask; she moved, burned hand curled against her chest, and the others fell in behind her — Kova with the multimeter, Ryla with the flashlight beam cutting dust, Mara carrying the clamp Jax had welded. The corridor hadn't been walked in weeks. Emergency strips glowed amber at ankle height, pulsing with the Bell's rhythm even though the Bell hadn't struck in hours. Or maybe it had, and no one was left to count.

At the access hatch, Kova knelt and pried the cover. The cable didn't run to the hub. It ran deeper, along a conduit Ines had never seen on any schematic, disappearing into the station's spine where the old manuscript archives were supposed to be — sealed since the first purge line. The pen-sound was louder here: scratch, pause, scratch, like something writing on paper that didn't want to be written on.

"Console's drawing from the archives," Kova said, not looking up. "Every page the figure held, every sheet we fed the slot — it's pulling them back through this line. Rewriting them. The draft stays open because it's still being written."

"By what?" Ryla asked.

The multimeter spiked. Kova swore, yanking her hand back as the cable jerked, alive, and a single sheet spat out of the conduit onto the grating at their feet. Ines picked it up. Her own handwriting, fresh as the signature she'd just gave, covered the page: *The vent holds at ninety. The audit counts. The writer pays.*

At the bottom, in a different hand — cramped, urgent, familiar — someone had scrawled: *Close the draft. Feed it the ending. Now.*

Ines read the note twice and hated the third reading for feeling like waiting. The handwriting was Lira’s—small, left-leaning, the way she wrote when she was trying not to wake the console—but the urgency was older than the conduit, older than the page, older than Lira getting added to the manifest at all.

She folded the fresh sheet over the note, made the correction visible, and wrote beneath it in her own rough hand: *Close draft. Log unlogged. End mass.* Kova said the console took archive paper, and the sheet had come up through the spine, so maybe it qualified. Tam leaned over the feed slot and started the protocol speech. Ines held up her burned hand. “Protocol wrote the override. I’m the signatory. The audit goes to me.” The synthetic voice came back, flat and unhurried. “Override accepted. Auditing cost.” The vent held ninety. Ines slid the sheet into the feed slot. Kova watched the multimeter. The cable took the paper. The console typed: *revision accepted. mass recalibrating.*

The draft closed with a sound like a spine cracking. The pen-sound died mid-scratch, as if the writer had been interrupted. The console’s lowercase light blinked once, then went dark. Kova swore and pulled the feed port cover closed. Tam exhaled hard. Mara looked at the vent. It was still holding ninety, but the scrubber alarm that had been blinking since the override had stopped blinking too. Ines felt the win in her chest and distrusted it immediately, because the synthetic voice had already said the audit was counting. The cost bill would come. The figure in the corridor—still holding its blank paper, still wearing pod four’s jumpsuit—turned its head toward the spine access hatch.

The figure held the turn like it had practiced. Its blank paper stayed flat against its chest, and the collar of pod four’s jumpsuit pulled tight across its throat. The neck gave a dry click, then locked. It faced the spine access hatch, and Ines read it wrong for half a second: it wasn’t looking at the hatch. It was looking at the dark mouth of the conduit, the place where the paper had gone.

Kova knelt at the hatch’s lip, one hand on the safety dog, breath loud in the quiet. The dog had no light behind it, or Ines couldn’t see one. The vent hummed above them, steady enough to be a lie. Ines felt the burn in her hand and hated that it made her slow. She kept her eyes on the figure.

“You gave it the corridor,” the figure said, and the voice came from the blank paper, or the jumpsuit speaker, or the station’s bad acoustics—in Ines’s voice, her burned-hand hitch, Lira’s urgency caught in it. “You gave it the ending.”

Ines didn’t flinch. Flinching was for people who hadn’t already signed. “I signed for the figure,” she said. “You took the signature.”

The figure took one step toward the spine access hatch. Paper dragged once on the floor. It stopped with its weight on the heel, not the toe, and the safety dog stared back with no light behind it.
